Love supplies the aim against teaching that produces empty disputes

Verse 3 tells Timothy to command certain people to stop. Verse 4 says their teaching produces disputes and not God’s work in faith. Verse 5 gives the goal of the command, and it is love. That love has three sources: a pure heart, a good conscience, and sincere faith. Verse 6 says some have missed these and turned to empty talk. So the test of teaching here is what it produces. Verse 19 repeats two of the three: faith and a good conscience.
Prayer for everyone leads into instructions shaped by unequal roles

Verse 1 asks prayer “for all men,” and verse 2 names kings. Verse 4 gives the reason: God desires all people to be saved. Verse 5 supports that with two “ones.” There is one God, so no people has a different one. There is one mediator between God and humans, the man Christ Jesus. Verse 6 completes it: he gave himself as a ransom for all. One God and one mediator for all is why prayer covers all.
Care for a household becomes a test of care for the assembly

Verse 4 requires an overseer to rule his own house well. Verse 5 gives the reason as a question in brackets. One who cannot rule his own house cannot care for God’s assembly. The comparison rests on a picture stated in verse 15. The assembly is called the house of God. So the smaller house shows how he will act in the larger one. The verbs differ: “rule” for the house, “take care of” for the assembly.
Received gifts and visible conduct answer restrictions and contempt for youth

Verse 3 names two rules of these teachers: no marriage and certain foods forbidden. Verse 4 answers with creation. Every creature of God is good. Nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving. The condition matters: the food is received as a gift. Verse 5 says it is made holy by God’s word and prayer. Verse 3 already said God created these foods to be received.
Family duties and tested testimony shape care and correction

Verse 3 says to honor widows “who are widows indeed.” Verse 4 puts the first duty on children and grandchildren. Caring for a parent is called piety and repayment. It is “acceptable in the sight of God.” Verse 8 says one who will not provide has denied the faith. Verse 16 gives the purpose: the assembly can then relieve widows who are alone.
Contentment and generous use answer the pursuit of wealth as religious gain

Verses 9–10 warn those who want to be rich. Verse 17 then speaks to those who already are. It tells them where not to put hope: in uncertain riches. Verse 18 says what to do with wealth, in four phrases. Do good, be rich in good works, be ready to give, be willing to share. The word “rich” is turned: the wealth that counts is good works. Verse 19 calls this a good foundation for the time to come.
